match.reason: The closest bank point, financing a new business, contrasts equity with debt for start-ups, which is a related but different idea from internal sources of finance such as retained profits in an existing business.

draft.title: Internal sources of finance
card: Internal finance is money that comes from inside the business. The business does not need to ask an outside lender or investor.
money the owner puts in from personal savings. In a company, this is the money its owners put in when they buy shares.
profits the business keeps and reinvests instead of paying them out to owners. They only exist once the business has made a profit.
Internal finance has no interest to pay and gives outsiders no say in the business. It may be limited, because it depends on what the owner can afford and how much profit the business has made.
draft.remember: Internal finance comes from within and costs no interest, but the amount may be small.

a.q: Which of these is an example of internal finance?
opts: Profits that a business keeps and reinvests
A loan from a bank, repaid with interest
Money raised by selling shares to new investors
An overdraft on the business's bank account
a.why: Retained profits are earned by the business and kept inside it, so no outside party is involved. The bank loan and the overdraft come from a lender, and new investors are outsiders, so none of those three is internal.
a.clue: Which source needs no outside lender or investor?

b.q: Priya runs a bakery in Orange. She wants a new oven, but the bakery made only a small profit this year. Why might internal finance not cover the cost?
opts: Retained profits and her savings may be too small
Internal finance must be repaid with interest
Internal finance gives outsiders a share of ownership
Internal finance can only be used for day-to-day costs
b.why: Internal finance depends on the profit the bakery has made and on what Priya can afford to put in, so it may be too small for a large purchase. It carries no interest and brings in no outside owners, so the other options describe things it does not do.
b.clue: Think about where the money comes from and how much there may be.

a.best: Profits that a business keeps and reinvests

b.best: Retained profits and her savings may be too small

problems.detail: The card says that in a company, owner's contribution is the money owners put in when they buy shares. This clashes with point 4, which treats selling shares as equity finance, an external source. It also clashes with question a, where money from selling shares to new investors is meant to be wrong. Students could not tell when share money counts as internal.

The right option is the only one with a hedge ('may be too small'). Every distractor uses an absolute word ('must', 'only') or a flat claim, so a student could pick the answer without knowing the idea.

money the owner puts in from personal savings, such as a sole trader using savings to buy stock. It comes from the owner, not from a lender or a new investor.
profits the business keeps and reinvests instead of paying them out to owners. They only exist once the business has made a profit.
Internal finance has no interest to pay and gives outsiders no say in the business. It may be limited, because it depends on what the owner can afford and how much profit the business has made.

b.q: Priya runs a bakery in Orange. She wants a new oven, but the bakery made only a small profit this year. Why might internal finance not cover the cost?
opts: It depends on profit and savings, which are small here
